title: An individualised approach to autism and criminal intent
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is treated in forensic evaluations of criminal intent and proposes an individualised, functional standard for weighing ASD-related evidence. Design/methodology/approach The paper synthesises recent empirical literature on ASD and social cognition, emotional regulation, adaptive functioning, suggestibility and threat perception and examines Virginia’s evidentiary statute on ASD and specific intent as an illustration of an individualised functional legal framework. Findings Diagnosis alone provides insufficient information about criminal intent. Autism-related differences in social cognition, emotional regulation and adaptive functioning are heterogeneous and only loosely tied to diagnostic status, so forensic relevance depends on documented, individualised impairment rather than the presence of an ASD diagnosis. Originality/value The paper integrates findings on theory of mind and criminal-intent recognition and on adaptive functioning in forensic ASD samples, with Virginia’s statutory framework to propose an individualised functional approach evaluators can apply directly to casework.
